Mockup for sign-off · 26 August 2026

The project header

You asked for a project’s three opening facts — the brief, the stakeholders, and the start and end dates — given a proper structure at the top of the page. Both proposals below are the real platform, not a drawing: the header block was replaced in the running page, so everything around it is the build you have.

Corrected after your note. You were right that the table ran off the edge, and the cause is worth knowing before anyone builds this: the platform sets a global table { min-width: 620px } so its data tables never squash. The grid column was 320px the whole time — the table overflowed its own track by exactly 300px. It needs min-width: 0, and the capture now asserts every element sits inside the pane rather than only that the page does not scroll sideways.

You have found a real gap, not just a layout preference. A project’s start and end are stored, and they appear in exactly one place in the whole product — the review deck. Neither the plan pane, the Performance pane nor the Reporting pane shows when a project runs, so the one page where you author a project cannot tell you its dates. The overrun note at the bottom is the only thing that mentions the end date, and only when a milestone overshoots it.

Today— brief as prose, stakeholders as chips, no dates at all

Two headings and a paragraph. It is not badly laid out — it is just that three facts of different shapes are being presented as three unrelated things, and the two dates are not presented at all.

A— a facts strip above the brief

One bordered row of four cells, in the same label / value idiom the score cards already use, with the brief as prose beneath it. Owner and Timeline move off the band into the strip — otherwise the header says the owner twice. It reads cleanly and costs one row of vertical space.

C— brief and stakeholders left, the facts as a table rightRecommended

The brief stays prose because that is what it is, the stakeholders stay chips because that is what they are, and the facts that are genuinely a table become one — label and value, four rows, in the product’s own quiet ground. It costs no vertical space at all: the table sits in the room the brief was already leaving empty on the right.

What decides it— the same two, at 1000px

Your laptop is 1000px, so this is the width that matters. A’s strip grows to three lines, because a cell’s height is the row’s height and “Finance Department, IT Department” will not fit in a quarter of the pane — the exact complaint that made every setup table one line per row. C stacks: the table drops below the brief and every value stays on one line.

A — three lines tall

C — stacks, one line per value

If you pick C, here is what it costs and what it needs

  • The band sheds the owner and the timeline pill, keeping the code and the name. One fact, one place — but it is a visible change to a header you see on every project, so it is the part to look at twice.
  • The pen has to edit start and end. They arrive by upload today and there is no way to correct one on the page. Showing a field nobody can fill is worse than not showing it — if we draw them, they get inputs in edit mode.
  • The three panes should agree. The dates belong on Performance and Reporting too, or the same project says different things depending on which tab you are on. Same block, read-only on those two.
  • It needs min-width: 0 and table-layout: fixed, or the platform’s global 620px table minimum pushes it 300px past the pane — which is exactly what you spotted.
  • Nothing new is stored. Owner, start, end, timeline and stakeholders all exist already; this only puts them on the page that authors them.
